title: Tokenizer pool orchestration and prefix-aware KV cache keying (WIP)
content:
Purpose
This doc collects design notes for a tokenizer-side orchestration layer and a prefix-aware KV-cache keying scheme that together aim to reduce observed tokenization tail latency and improve cache hit stability for multi-tenant workloads. It's a working doc capturing tradeoffs, instrumentation, and an experiment plan; not final design.

Background & motivation
We get two recurring production pain points: (1) occasional high tail latency from tokenization when large requests arrive or when cold tokenizer processes spin up, and (2) cache fragmentation in the KV cache when token boundaries in client requests vary slightly (e.g., different whitespace, casing, or control chars), which reduces prefix cache hit rates and increases per-token cost. Current approach uses per-request tokenization in the serving process and a KV cache keyed by raw token-id sequences, which is brittle across small canonicalization differences.

Goals
- Reduce 95/99th percentile tokenization time without increasing median CPU cost.
- Stabilize KV cache hit rate across semantically-equivalent prefix variations.
- Keep the runtime change surface small so rollout can be staged per-cluster.
- Preserve per-customer isolation and allow per-model tokenizer profiles.

Non-goals
- This doc does not propose replacing model tokenization logic (we assume the model tokenizer implementation remains authoritative).
- No major changes to public API; aim for server-side only optimizations.

High-level proposal
Two complementary components: (A) Tokenizer Worker Pool with request scheduling and warm preloads, and (B) Prefix-normalized KV cache keying with lightweight edit normalization.

A) Tokenizer Worker Pool and Scheduler
- Separate process pool: move tokenization out of the main serving worker into a small pool of tokenizer worker processes per node (or per tenant for high-tier customers). Each worker loads model tokenizers (tokenizer graphs, merges, vocab) in-process and exposes an IPC RPC (unix socket / fast gRPC) to the serving runtime.
- Worker lifecycle: keep a fixed-size pool with LRU eviction of tokenizer contexts. A context = (model_id, tokenizer_variant). Size defaults to N=6 per node (configurable). Cold-start penalty is reduced by keeping the most-used tokenizers resident.
- Scheduling: incoming request route -> lookup best-matching tokenizer context -> if resident, dispatch to worker with priority tagging; if not, either (i) schedule a background preload (if request priority is low) and do on-demand tokenization in the serving worker as fallback, or (ii) if request is high-priority, block the request briefly (configurable cutoff e.g., 50ms) to allow tokenizer to load into pool.
- Priority buckets: realtime (low latency SLO), batch (throughput), background (async preloads). Realtime requests get queued only short durations; batch requests can be scheduled to shared tokenizer workers to increase batching.
- Tokenizer batching: the tokenizer workers should accept micro-batches of strings for a single model/tokenizer to amortize tokenization overhead (particularly for short prompts). Serving runtime should aggregate tokenization requests for same tokenizer within a 5-10ms window. This trades tiny added latency at the median for large throughput gains and lower CPU overhead at tail.
- Opportunistic warm preloads: use traffic heatmaps to proactively load tokenizers during quiet windows (off-peak) and after deploys. Also, when a request arrives with a model variant not resident, enqueue a preload if observed request frequency for that model in last 60s > threshold.
- Isolation and quota: per-tenant resource budgets for tokenizer workers; burstable limits. For Dedicated/private deployments we expose pool size and residency policy as an operator knob.

B) Prefix-aware KV cache keying
Problem: exact token-id sequence keys create many near-duplicate entries. Idea: canonicalize prefixes and apply a normalized key prefix hashing so that small surface differences map to the same cache lineage.

- Normalization steps (cheap, server-side): trim leading/trailing whitespace, collapse multiple internal spaces to single space, normalize line endings to 
, apply Unicode NFKC normalization, and lowercase only if tokenizer config indicates case-insensitive usage. We will not attempt aggressive semantic normalization (e.g., stopword removal) to avoid model regression.
- Token-aware hashing: compute cache keys from token-id prefixes but also attach a normalized-text fingerprint. Key = H(model_id || tokenizer_variant || norm_fingerprint || token_prefix_hash_windowed). The token_prefix_hash_windowed uses a rolling hash over last K tokens (configurable, default K=64) so that long prefixes don't explode key size while keeping near-prefix alignment.
- Prefix bucketing: to reduce fragmentation we support a bucketed namespace: bucket_id = H(norm_fingerprint || first-M-tokens) mod B. This allows eviction and local metrics per bucket and reduces noisy neighbors.
- Fuzzy prefix match fallback: on a miss, try up to 2 neighboring bucket probes using similarity heuristics (small edit-distance on the normalized text) before doing a full model decode. This increases CPU slightly on misses but dramatically reduces redundant cache population.

Instrumentation & metrics to add
- Tokenizer worker metrics: resident_context_count, load_time_ms, queue_length, avg_batch_size, cpu_ms_per_token, peak_rss_mb, failed_loads.
- Scheduling metrics: blocked_requests_by_priority, avg_lock_wait_ms, preload_hits (requests that were served after preload finished), coldfallbacks (requests served in-process because pool full).
- Cache metrics: prefix_hit_rate (per-model), bucket_hit_rate, probe_success_rate (for fuzzy probes), normalized_collision_rate.
- End-to-end: tokenization_latency_{p50,p95,p99}, total_request_latency_{p50,p95,p99} for same SLO buckets pre/post rollout.

Safety and failure modes
- If tokenizer worker pool becomes unreachable, fallback to existing in-process tokenization path with rate limiting to avoid thundering herd.
- If normalization causes a measurable regression in output quality (measured via eval prompt set), we have a kill switch to disable normalization per-model. We must tie this to rollout gates.
- Memory leak watch: tokenizer libraries historically retain memory after certain tokenizers are used. Enforce periodic cycling of workers (graceful restart) and monitor peak RSS.

Testing & experiment plan
Phase 0: Microbenchmarks (local)
- Run tokenizer microbenchmarks across top 10 models: cold load time, tokenize throughput, batch amortization curve, memory footprint.
Phase 1: Canary node rollout (internal test cluster)
- Enable pool with small N, no normalization; measure p99 tokenization latency and CPU. Validate fallback paths.
Phase 2: Normed cache + bucketed keys behind feature flag for 5% traffic
- Run A/B measuring prefix_hit_rate, downstream token decode cost, and evaluate quality-sensitive prompts for regressions.
Phase 3: Gradual ramp to 100% with heuristics tuned and operator knobs exposed.

Open questions and trade-offs
- Pool size heuristic: per-node fixed N vs dynamic proportional to node memory. Start with fixed then consider auto-sizing.
- Aggressiveness of normalization: more normalization improves cache but risks quality drift. Must be gated per model and validated by automated evals.
- Complexity of fuzzy probes: more probes reduce population cost but add compute on miss. We need threshold-based probes.

Action items (short-term)
- Aisha: spin up microbench harness for tokenizer variants (due 2025-01-21).
- Mateo: prototype small IPC tokenizer worker with batching API (WIP PR linked).
- Chen: add instrumentation hooks in KV cache to emit bucket-level metrics.
- Priya: define evaluation prompt sets for normalization regression testing.

Notes to reviewers
- This doc intentionally keeps the public API unchanged; changes are server-side and operators can toggle features per-deployment. Feedback welcome on the normalization pipeline and on probe budget suggestions.

References
- internal tokenizer microbenchmarks (linked in linked_artifacts)
- prior docs: we deliberately avoid duplicating the handoff and incremental prefetch proposals; this doc focuses on pooling and cache-key stability.
